Recognition as the Felt Re-Cognition of the Self

The Authoritative Statement from the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī

With its Expansion of Utpaladeva's Kārikās and its Correction and Completion of Ratié's Reconstruction

  • his is the authoritative recognition source. It states the Pratyabhijñā thesis — recognition
  • pratyabhijñā*) is the felt re-cognition of the self — from the deepest source that survives: the
  • varapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (IPVV) of Abhinavagupta, in a complete new translation. It shows,

  • lt is distinguished from the ground.*

PART ONE — THE THESIS AND ITS SOURCES

1. The thesis, stated with its full support

itself as the Lord — the removal of a false self-positioning, and nothing added.**

  • d forgotten — not a new fact, but a return. Ratié's finding that recognition "produces no new
  • owledge" (Ch. Conclusion) is the same point.
  • Itself as the Lord (ātmā īśvara). The self that is re-cognized is not a mere finite ego but

  • the essence of light (IPK 1.5.11). The felt is not a side-effect; it is the register of the
  • cognition.

2. The honesty rule

  • is source holds itself to the discipline that the recognition-thesis demands of its own proponents.
  • e Pratyabhijñā is a metaphysics; but its method is anti-dogmatic — it argues, in the nanu (objection)
  • āha (reply) rhythm, against every rival. The essay follows suit:
  • No tradition may inherit another's conclusion merely because they share a structure. The felt is
  • ared with naturalism; only the ground is the Pratyabhijñā's addition. This distinction is kept
  • roughout, and it is the source of the essay's final honesty (§VIII).

  • es not, by itself, prove one universal consciousness. The IPVV argues the ground more strongly than
  • e secondary literature allows — but the final universalization remains the commitment, and this
  • say marks it as such.

PART TWO — THE ROOT (THE IPK)

3. What the IPK is

  • e Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā ("The Stances on the Recognition of the Lord") of Utpaladeva (fl. c.
  • 5–975 CE) is a short text of some fifty-five kārikās in four adhikāras (books):
  • Āgamādhikāra (Book I) — the root of the recognition philosophy.
  • Jñānādhikāra (Book II) — cognition.
  • Kriyādhikāra (Book III) — action.
  • Tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra (Book IV) — the collection of the thirty-six categories.
  • e IPK is the root text. Everything else — the IPVV, the essay, the whole Pratyabhijñā school — is a
  • mmentary on, or reconstruction of, this root. And a crucial fact established by the Torella volume is
  • at Utpaladeva, not Abhinavagupta, is the real innovator — the Vivṛti (Utpaladeva's lost
  • to-commentary) is "the real centre of gravity of the system," and most of Abhinavagupta's ideas are
  • e development of what Utpaladeva had already expounded. This matters for citation practice: the
  • esis originates in the IPK; the IPVV is its deepest unfolding.

4. The root kārikās that carry the thesis

4.1 IPK 1.5.11 — vimarśa is the essence of light (the reflexivity claim)

  • e single most important kārikā for this essay. It states the reflexivity claim — that the essence
  • consciousness is not a passive showing but a felt self-awareness:
"The essential nature of light is reflective awareness (vimarśa); otherwise light, though 'coloured'
by objects, would be similar to an insentient reality, such as crystal and so on."
  • e Vṛtti adds the decisive gloss: reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) is the primary essence
  • mukhya ātman*) of light, "since there is no savouring (camatkṛteḥ)." The point:
  • A light that merely showed the world but did not know that it showed it would be no different
  • om a crystal — it would reflect the blue, the yellow, the jar, but not be aware of reflecting.
  • What makes the light conscious — what makes it not a thing — is that it is present to itself in
  • e act of manifesting.
  • And that self-presence is a savouring, a camatkṛti — a felt, not merely formal, reflexivity.
  • is is the seed of the whole thesis: consciousness is not a showing but a felt showing. The felt
  • -cognition is not imported into the system from outside; it is here in the root, as the very essence
  • light.

4.2 IPK 1.3.7 — the three powers (the structure of the subject)

  • e self that is thus self-aware is not featureless. It is a single reality with three constitutive
  • wers:
"There would be one reality whose nature is consciousness, possessing the powers of cognition,
memory, and exclusion" (jñāna-smṛti-apohana-śaktimān).
  • ree points:
  • Constitutive, not accidental. The powers are not things the self has; they are the very
  • ructure of the self's operation. The self just is the act of knowing, remembering, and excluding.
  • Apohana is the Śaiva transformation of the Buddhist apoha. For the Buddhists, apoha is a
  • gative operation of language ("cow" = "not-non-cow"); for Utpaladeva, it is a positive power of
  • termination — the delimiting by which the self knows what it is not. The power of exclusion is
  • at makes conceptual thought possible; it is not secondary but one of the three fundamental powers.
  • The triad is jñāna-smṛti-apoha, not icchā-jñāna-kriyā. This distinction is not pedantic. The
  • K's constitutive triad is the epistemic one — the structural account of the subject. The
  • litional triad (will-knowledge-action) is a later, prefatory gloss. The IPVV's own anatomy
  • nfirms this (§VI): the jñānādhikāra is organized around exactly the jñāna-smṛti-apoha triad, in
  • at order.

4.3 IPK 1.2.1–6 — the Buddhist pūrvapakṣa (the debate's textual source)

  • e IPK opens with the hardest rival — the Buddhist no-self argument. Ratié's Ch. 1 reconstructs it:
  • e perception-of-Self argument (IPK 1.2.1–2) and the inference-of-Self / memory argument (IPK
  • 2.3–6). The debate the whole recognition-thesis engages is here in the root. The IPVV will run this
  • rvapakṣa in full (§V).

4.4 Camatkāra is Utpaladeva's concept

  • is sometimes supposed that the felt register of the doctrine — the savouring, the wonder, the bliss
  • is an Abhinavagupta addition. The Torella volume establishes the contrary:
"Precisely to Utpaladeva we do owe the entrance of aesthetics into philosophical-religious
speculation. His concept of camatkāra (wondrous enjoyment) marks a higher level of experience, which
leaves the reality and beauty of the manifested world intact, but at the same time projects it into a
totality whose centre is Supreme Consciousness."
  • e felt re-cognition is thus in the root. It is Utpaladeva's own concept, not a later addition.

5. What the root leaves open

  • e root states the thesis in seed. But it leaves open the questions this essay answers from the IPVV:
  • Does the reflexivity claim have an argument? The IPK asserts that vimarśa is the essence; the
  • VV argues it (§VI).
  • Is the "I" a construction? The IPK says the self has the powers; the IPVV proves the "I" is not
  • construction (§VI).
  • What is the ground? The IPK implies the one; the IPVV argues it via the order-less support (§VIII).
  • How does one attain it? The IPK gestures; the IPVV gives the soteriology (§VII).
  • e root is the seed; the IPVV is the full tree. This essay's task is to show how the tree grows from
  • e seed — and, where Ratié reconstructed the tree from fallen leaves, to measure the reconstruction
  • ainst the living whole.

PART THREE — THE COMPASS (RATIÉ'S RECONSTRUCTION)

6. What Ratié's Le Soi et l'Autre does

  • abelle Ratié's *Le Soi et l'Autre: Identité, différence et altérité dans la philosophie de la
  • atyabhijñā* (Brill, 2011) is the most rigorous modern reconstruction of the Pratyabhijñā. Working
  • om the IPK, its Vṛtti, and the fragments of the lost Vivṛti, Ratié reconstructs the doctrine with
  • ilological care and philosophical precision. Her book is organized around the paradox of
  • lf-recognition: we recognize our face, our past, our thought — but what is it to recognize oneself?
  • r findings converge exactly on the root thesis, and they are worth stating before the IPVV is brought
  • rward, so that the measure of the IPVV's further reach is clear.

7. Ratié's findings, chapter by chapter

7.1 Ch. 1 — The Buddhist critique of the Self

  • tié reconstructs the Buddhist no-self (anātmavāda) position that the rest of the book refutes — the
  • K's Buddhist pūrvapakṣa. The hardest rival denies the Self; but self-luminosity (svaprakāśa) is
  • hared* — the debate is whether it implies a Self. Recognition is an ordinary felt cognition.
"la conscience ne s'y vise donc pas objectivement… mais s'y sait être sur un mode parfaitement
immédiat ou 'non positionnel'." (Consciousness knows itself in a non-positional mode.)

7.2 Ch. 2 — Cognitive synthesis

  • e Buddhist has shown no Self; Ratié shows the Pratyabhijñā's answer: the Self is needed for the
  • nthesis of cognitions. Without a persisting subject, memory and recognition across moments are
  • possible. Memory is re-appropriation (never truly lost); vimarśa is latent in every perception; the
  • nthesizing self is non-objective — "blind, deaf, mute" cognitions cannot unify themselves.
"cette 'synthèse des formes antérieure et postérieure du Je'… par laquelle le sujet percevant se
saisit à la fois comme la conscience d'où émerge l'objet et comme la conscience où il se résorbe."
(The synthesis of the anterior and posterior forms of the I.)

7.3 Ch. 3 — The absolute subject (IPK 1.3.7) ⚠️ corrected

  • e core positive claim. Ratié centers this on IPK 1.3.7 — the "heart of the treatise." And here this
  • oject has made a correction, confirmed by the IPVV's own structure: 1.3.7 is the jñāna–smṛti–apoha
  • iad (knowledge, memory, exclusion) — "possessing the powers of knowledge, memory and exclusion" —
  • NOT** the icchā/jñāna/kriyā triad. The volitional triad is the prefatory/structural reading, not the
  • xt of 1.3.7. The IPVV's jñānādhikāra is organized around exactly the jñāna-smṛti-apoha triad, in
  • at order (§VI).

7.4 Ch. 4 — The Self, the cognitions, their relation

  • e "I" is a cognition of recognition (pratyabhijñāpratyaya); recognition is *experience, not
  • nstruction*; identity = dynamism; the never-lost identity.
"une reconnaissance (pratyabhijñā) qui… n'est pas une pure et simple construction abstraite, mais
une expérience." (Recognition is an experience, not an abstract construction.)

7.5 Ch. 5 — Common idealism

  • iva and Buddhist idealism share consciousness-fundamental. The shared ākāra thesis implies a
  • rmanent subject; the object is re-cognized as one's own luminous self (tādātmya).
"Il y a donc une identité (tādātmya) foncière du reflet et du miroir… hors du miroir, le reflet
n'est rien." (The fundamental identity of reflection and mirror.)

7.6 Ch. 6 — The mirror, the dreamer, and the yogin (IPK 1.5.1–9)

  • e famous chapter. Consciousness creates (yogin) not reveals (lamp/mirror); freedom is established
  • self-awareness, not hypothesis. The key image: the yogin — for the Śaiva, consciousness does not
  • rely reveal (like a lamp) but creates (like a yogin projecting).
"cidātmaiva hi devo 'ntaḥsthitam icchāvaśād bahiḥ / yogīva nirupādānam arthajātam prakāśayet."
(Like a yogin, consciousness manifests its objects by its free will, without material cause.)

7.7 Ch. 7 — Freedom (svātantrya) ⭐ the load-bearing chapter

  • eedom is the essence; vimarśa = freedom + felicity + wonder; identity = freedom to become Other;
  • ienation = misrecognition of freedom.
"camatkāra… c'est la divine surprise… dans laquelle on s'étonne moins de l'objet lui-même que de la
satisfaction qu'on se découvre éprouver à son égard." (*The satisfaction one discovers oneself
feeling.*)

7.8 Ch. 8 — The other: solipsism or intersubjectivity?

  • e other is recognized (not inferred) as my own subjectivity outside myself; resists objectivation;
  • nism founds compassion.
"être conscient de l'existence d'autrui, c'est reconnaître hors de soi sa propre subjectivité."
(Being conscious of the other's existence is recognizing one's own subjectivity outside oneself.)

  • fference is real yet non-dual — the deployment of the Self's dynamic essence, an upāya; the
  • nfinitesimal gap from oneself."

  • e solution (freedom); identity = freedom-to-become-other; recognition = the return that shows (not

"on ne produit aucune connaissance nouvelle chez cet individu." (One produces no new knowledge.)
"Le traité… ne démontre pas ; il montre." (The treatise does not demonstrate; it shows.)

9. Where Ratié stops

PART FOUR — THE AUTHORITY (THE IPVV)

10. What the IPVV is

  • e Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī of Abhinavagupta is his enormous commentary on Utpaladeva's
  • ostly lost) Vivṛti — some thirty-four thousand lines across three volumes. It is organized as a
  • nning commentary on the IPK, glossing each kārikā and then arguing, in the nanu (objection) → āha
  • eply) rhythm that gives the text its dialectical texture.
  • The structure (the IPVV's own anatomy):**
  • `
  • l 1 (M00020) jñānādhikāra — the upoddhāta, the self-as-Lord, memory, the reflexion core
  • l 2 (M00021) jñānādhikāra — the caturtho → aṣṭamo vimarśas: memory/aham, the jñānaśakti
  • anifestation), the smṛti/apohana, the one-support
  • l 3 (M00022) kriyādhikāra — the action-section (ending the kāryakāraṇabhāvavimarśa)
  • amādhikāra — the teaching-section (the śivatattva, the padārthavarga)
  • ttvādhikāra — the categories-section (the closing sum, the ||samāptā||)
  • `
  • The nanu→āha skeleton.** The IPVV's whole texture is dialectical — every passage is an objection
  • anu) met by a reply (āha), usually against the Buddhist, the Vaiśeṣika/Kāṇāda, the Advaitin, or the
  • ṃkhya. This is the IPVV's own internal rhythm, and it is the first thing that distinguishes the IPVV
  • om the IPK: where the IPK states, the IPVV argues.
  • Why it is the authority.** The IPVV is the deepest primary source for the doctrine, and it survives
  • hole*. Where Ratié reconstructs, the IPVV states and argues. This essay therefore treats the IPVV as
  • thoritative and checks the reconstruction against it.

11. The three registers of the recognition-thesis

  • e IPVV states the recognition-thesis not once but at three distinct registers. That it does so is
  • self evidence that the thesis is the heart of the system: the same move, at three levels, is not an
  • casional claim but the structure of the whole. And — decisively — all three registers are the *same
  • ve*: content unchanged, positioning changed.

11.1 Register 1 — Foregrounding (V1E)

  • e first register is spatial. Against the Buddhist's worry that recognition must establish
  • mething, the IPVV insists it merely foregrounds what is already there:
"The pramāṇa here is not establishing something new. It is foregrounding what is already present
but hidden. The recognition does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always
near and always present, into the foreground of our own awareness."
  • e recognition changes where the self stands in the field of awareness — from an instrument lost among
  • e things of the body and the world to the primary thing seen. Nothing is added; the same content is
  • -arranged. This is the removal thesis in its simplest form: the false self-positioning (the self
  • a thing among things) is removed, and the self stands where it always was.

11.2 Register 2 — The "I was never not" (V1D)

  • e second register is temporal, and it grounds the removal in the eternity of the self:
"The manifestation of the self is not unprecedented. It does not begin to shine at some moment; it
was always shining… The self is un-cut by all three times: past, present, and future. It did not
come into being, and it will not pass away."
  • cause the self was never absent, there is nothing for recognition to add — nothing could be added to
  • eternal self. The "unprecedented manifestation," the appearance of something new, is only apparent;
  • rests on the eternal, always-manifested knower. Here the removal thesis is grounded: recognition
  • nnot be an attainment, because the self never was not.

11.3 Register 3 — The lover-union (V3P)

  • e third register is aesthetic and relational, and it ties the thesis to the felt:
"The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman; but as long as he is not recognized, he cannot
be enjoyed. So the world-Lord, always present, always near, is not experienced in his own splendor
until the recognition arises… The single act of recognition turns the un-known nearness into the joy
of union."
  • e lover is near — the content is present, never absent. What changes with recognition is the
  • lation: from un-known nearness to the joy of union. And this change is felt — it is the joy, the
  • vouring, the camatkāra. The recognition does not bring the lover; it turns the near into the
  • joyed. This is the removal thesis in its fullest form: the felt re-cognition.

11.4 The three are one

  • regrounding (spatial), "I was never not" (temporal-eternal), lover-union (relational-aesthetic): all
  • ree are content unchanged, positioning changed. This is the thesis of this essay, stated in the
  • thority itself at three registers. The recognition is not the addition of a content but the
  • -positioning of the self — and, in the third register, that re-positioning is experienced as a felt
  • y. **The felt re-cognition is not a metaphor imposed on the system; it is the system's own statement,
  • its deepest source.**

PART FIVE — THE EXPANSION OF THE IPK (WHAT THE IPVV ADDS TO THE ROOT)

  • e IPVV is not merely a commentary; it is an expansion. Where the IPK states, the IPVV argues;
  • ere the IPK asserts, the IPVV proves. This part shows, systematically, how the IPVV expands the root
  • rikās.

12. The expansion of the reflexivity claim (IPK 1.5.11 → the vimarśa as the heart)

  • e IPK states that vimarśa is the essence of light. The IPVV expands this into the heart of the whole
  • ctrine (V2H):
"The manifestation (prakāśa) is not a passive, inert light. Its very nature is the *reflexive-
awareness* (vimarśa) — the light's own grasp of itself. Without the vimarśa, the manifestation would
be like crystal: it would show the world, but it would not know that it showed it; it would be inert.
What makes the light light — what makes it consciousness and not a thing — is that it is aware of
itself in the very act of manifesting."
  • What the IPVV adds:** the proof. The IPK asserts the reflexivity claim; the IPVV proves it by the
  • ift-action argument — in quick reading, rapid motion, hurried speech, we abandon and seize without
  • using to reflect, yet these acts are preceded by a re-reflection (parāmarśa), and this shows the
  • ower and the known are not two separate things but one act of the self-aware consciousness (V2H).
  • e swift act is the empirical proof that reflexivity is intrinsic, not an added second act.
  • And the identification with the supreme Word.** The IPVV identifies the reflexive-awareness with the
  • rā-vāk, the supreme speech:
"This self-knowing is the parā-vāk, the supreme speech, from which all the lower levels of speech
(the madhyamā, the vaikharī) descend. It is the Lord's freedom (svātantrya) and his lordship
(aiśvarya)." (V2H)

  • th freedom — a systematic identification the root only implies.

(smṛti) → self-knowledge (apohana) → self-expression (kriyā). Each presupposes the previous. The
order of the vimarśas IS the order of the self's unfolding." (the internal arc)

PART SIX — THE ARGUMENT (THE IPVV'S PROOF OF THE INTRINSIC "I")

  • is is the heart of the essay's claim that the IPVV goes further than Ratié. Ratié reports that
  • cognition removes a mis-knowledge; the IPVV argues the "I" that the removal presupposes.

18. The objection

  • e reflexive-awareness, the IPVV has said, is the manifestation's own nature. But the reflexive-
  • areness is word-joined — it takes the form of the word "I." And the word-joined, it might seem, is
  • construction (vikalpa). If the Lord's own self-awareness were a construction, it would be of the
  • āyā*-form, the saṃsāric — which cannot be. The objection is precise, and it threatens the whole
  • ctrine: does the felt "I" of recognition reduce to a mental construction?

19. The answer: the "I" is not a construction

  • e IPVV answers by defining construction and showing the "I" is none of it (V2L):
"The construction is of three kinds: it joins what is distinct (as one joins molasses, curd, and
pepper); it constructs the one in many ways; or it splits off a doubted, other form. All three are
operations of division and joining, of this-and-that. But the 'I'-recollection is none of these. It
does not join a distinct 'this' to a distinct 'I'; it is the single self-grasp, resting in itself. It
is the pure self-awareness that underlies every construction, the very thing that makes construction
possible, without itself being one."
  • The force of this is precise.** Construction, whatever else it is, is an operation on parts — it
  • ins distinct things, or multiplies a one, or splits off a doubted other. The "I"-grasp is none of
  • ese:
  • Construction joins distinct things → the "I" does not (it is not "this I" built from a distinct
  • his" and "I").
  • Construction constructs the one into many → the "I" does not (it is the one).
  • Construction splits off a doubted other → the "I" does not (it is the un-doubted foundation).
  • erefore the "I"-grasp is not a construction. And because every higher-order operation — every model,
  • ery self-attribution, every re-description of experience — is a joining or a splitting, the "I"-grasp
  • nnot be a higher-order operation at all. **It is the self-presence that higher-order operations
  • esuppose, the root that makes them possible without itself being one.**

20. The meeting of the structural rival

  • re the IPVV meets its deepest rival, and it does so not by refutation but by absorption. The rival's
  • sition — in its ancient Buddhist and its modern form — is that reflexivity is structural: experience
  • n include its own occurrence, can fold back and represent itself, and this folding is all the self
  • at exists. This is the position that Ñāṇavīra, in the modern Pāli tradition, states with great force,
  • d it carries a warning directed precisely at the Pratyabhijñā: that Abhinavagupta "converted the
  • flexive self-identity of a conditioned structure into an ultimately existing universal Self."
  • The IPVV's answer is not to deny that the folding occurs. It is to deny that the folding is the
  • ot.**
  • The structural reflexivity — experience folding back and including itself — is a *construction-
  • pacity*: it is the higher-order operation, the joining and splitting that the self-model theories
  • scribe.
  • The IPVV grants that this capacity exists. What it denies is that it is the root.
  • The "I"-grasp is not one more instance of the folding; it is the self-presence that the folding
  • esupposes — the "pure self-awareness that underlies every construction, the very thing that makes
  • nstruction possible, without itself being one."
  • Structural reflexivity is the folding; intrinsic self-manifestation is the self-grasp that the
  • lding serves.* In the terms of the modern debate: a self-model explains the *content of the "I" —
  • s self-attributions, its self-representation. It cannot explain the self-grasp that is aware of the
  • del as its own. The IPVV's argument is exactly this: the model is a construction; the "I"-recollection
  • what is not a construction; therefore the model cannot be the root of the "I." The rival describes
  • e capacity; the IPVV points to what the capacity presupposes.

21. The confirmation in the IPVV's own anatomy

  • at this is not a reading imposed on the text is confirmed by the IPVV's own structure. The
  • ānādhikāra is organized around exactly the triad the IPK states — jñāna-smṛti-apoha, in that order.
  • d the powers unfold in a necessary order: manifestation → persistence → self-knowledge →
  • lf-expression. The apohana is the pivot: it is the power by which the self excludes what is not
  • self, and its deepest result is the argument just given — that the "I" is not a construction. The
  • VV is not a loose collection of arguments; it is one arc, the powers unfolding in order, the
  • lf-awareness their root, and the whole converging on the one knower. The non-constructed "I" is not a
  • ngle proof; it is the pivot of the entire second volume.

PART SEVEN — WHERE THE IPVV GOES FURTHER THAN BOTH IPK AND RATIÉ

  • e IPVV is not just deeper on the root and the reconstruction; it adds whole regions that neither the
  • K nor Ratié's book (focused on the recognition/subject/other) develops. These are the essay's claim
  • originality: the IPVV's epistemology of action, its tattva-ontology, and its soteriology.

22. The kriyādhikāra: the epistemology and metaphysics of action (V3A–I)

  • tié's book is focused on the jñāna side — the subject, the other, identity. It treats action only in
  • ssing. The IPVV devotes a whole adhikāra to it:
  • V3A — Action, time, sequence: the timeless that manifests order. The Lord is beyond sequence, yet
  • nifests manifold sequences; the mirror shows order without division.
  • V3B — The action-cognitions as bhedābheda: "this is the very same body," the distinction-and-
  • n-distinction vimarśa.
  • V3C–F — The pramāṇavimarśa: the valid means operates on the appearance; error is a matter of the
  • flexive-awareness being un-contradicted; the knower is the ground of everything.
  • V3G–I — The kāryakāraṇatāvimarśa: causality is the conscious knower's agency. The inert
  • nnot be a cause; inference holds across knowers because the Lord creates the appearances as one;
  • e will is cause, agent, and action; the difference of things is real, not mere ignorance.
  • The crown of the kriyādhikāra (V3-I).** The deepest objection — if all is one, how is action
  • ssible? — is answered by the will-to-do (the parāmarśa that joins agent and object), and the
  • vaita's "un-explainable ignorance" is refuted:
"The one-form Brahman cannot have an ignorance that is the mere absence of something else. Nor can
the separate souls exist… If the ignorance is called 'un-explainable' (anirvācya), then we still do
not know whose it is; 'it shines and yet is un-explainable' is the speech of a yakṣa… Even if we
appeal to the revealed teaching, that teaching too would be ignorance."
  • This is a full epistemology and metaphysics of action that neither the IPK nor Ratié develops.** It
  • the essay's first "goes further" region.

23. The āgamādhikāra: the tattva-ontology (V3J–M)

PART EIGHT — THE DEEP CROSS-EXAMINATIONS (THE IPVV AGAINST THE RIVALS)

  • e pushing-ipvv sessions have hounded the IPVV against its rivals, forcing its own reasoning and
  • nding where it resolves, deepens, or hits the same wall. These cross-examinations are the essay's
  • versarial depth.

26. The IPVV vs. the Tantrāloka's cruxes

  • obing the IPVV with the Tantrāloka's tough cruxes reveals that the IPVV is the sharper, more
  • alectical work:
  • Crux | Tantrāloka | IPVV | Verdict |
  • -----|-----------|------|---------|
  • 1. Universality gap | asserted | argued (V2C sārūpya; V3C the blue-to-me-not-Caitra; V2G from-within) | RESOLVED better |
  • 2. Memory→identity | asserted | answered (V2L the non-constructed "I") | RESOLVED better |
  • 3. Karma vs. freedom | freedom-contracted | deepened (V3B the un-thwarted; true-by-stability-use) | resolved + sharpened |
  • 4. Two-levels | binary | threefold (satya/saṃvṛtisatya/asatya) | made more precise |
  • 5. Recognition | reversal of direction | foregrounding (V1E); the lover (V3P) | made concrete |
  • 6. Felt→ground | asserted | asserted (the one light) | SAME WALL |
  • The universality gap, resolved.** The Tantrāloka asserted the step from "manifest to me" to "the
  • iversal perceiver." The IPVV argues it (V3C): the blue appears "to me and not to Caitra" — and this
  • ry fact, which the Tantrāloka treated as the index of finitude, is inverted into the proof of
  • nsciousness as the ground. If the blue stood by its own power, it would shine for everyone; it shines
  • r me, so it stands by the power of consciousness. And "the one light rises, born of means, object and
  • ower" — the knower, means, and known are one act.
  • The memory→identity step, answered.** The Tantrāloka asserted a persisting subject. The IPVV answers
  • e mechanistic objection (V2L): source-attribution is a construction, but the "I" that the construction
  • rves is the non-constructed self-grasp. The mechanism explains the content of memory; it cannot
  • plain the non-constructed "I" that holds it together.
  • The two-levels, made precise.** The Tantrāloka's binary (ground/contraction) becomes, in the IPVV, a
  • reefold: satya (true), saṃvṛtisatya (conventional-true, "coordinate with the real"), asatya (untrue).
  • e conventional is not a fiction; it is real-but-not-substantial. This answers the reality-vs-illusion
  • jection more precisely than the Tantrāloka.
  • Recognition, made concrete.** The Tantrāloka said recognition is the reversal of direction; the IPVV
  • ys it is foregrounding — "not an instrument lost among the things, but the primary thing we see."
  • e lover-image is the master-key in aesthetic form.

27. The IPVV's co-opting of the Buddhist

  • ainst the Buddhist, Abhinavagupta does not refute; he co-opts. The Buddhist's own tools are
  • cepted and turned to the Śaiva conclusion:
  • The inference-theory (V2E): the Vijñānavādin uses the reflection to infer an external ground;
  • hinavagupta keeps the inference-structure but changes its conclusion — "even the error, being a
  • lation, is a pramā." The determination of the external is valid by its bond to the thing.
  • The other-minds inference (V2F): the Buddhist hopes to infer another's mind; Abhinavagupta uses
  • e Buddhist's own inference-rules (the candana/agni fragrance; the "being-gone-to-the-other" as
  • -inferable) to show the inference fails. Then: "the appearances alone suffice."
  • The dream (V2G) — the deepest co-opting: the Buddhist uses the dream to prove the world is
  • real; Abhinavagupta agrees the dream is uncaused but re-reads it — the dream proves that
  • nsciousness creates an object-mass by its will. The Buddhist's own example of illusion becomes
  • e proof of the creation-power.
  • Self-awareness (V2C): the Buddhist's own svasamvedana is adopted and deepened — cognition is
  • lf-luminous and never the object of another.
  • The meta-gem:** the co-opting reveals that the Buddhist and the Śaiva are *two readings of the same
  • arting point* — appearances (ābhāsa) as all we have. The Buddhist reads them negatively (unreal,
  • -self); the Śaiva reads them positively (the real self-articulation of consciousness). **The debate
  • not a clash of worldviews but a dispute over the valence of the same appearances.** The Buddhist is
  • t the enemy of the recognition-thesis but its co-owner of the starting point.

28. The recognition-formulations and the σ-flip

  • e IPVV's three registers of recognition (foregrounding, "I was never not," the lover-union) are the
  • me move at three registers — content unchanged, positioning changed. This is exactly the formal
  • flip (AM0): the tuple content identical, σ changes. The IPVV states our formalization at three
  • gisters, and the third (the lover) ties it to the felt/rasa.
  • d the IPVV supports the "internally manifested forms, not the filter" account (V2D: "to know a thing
  • to be the light"; V2G: "the Lord manifests the world from within himself"; V3C: "the one light rises,
  • rn of means, object and knower"). **Our formulation is not imposed on the IPVV; it IS the IPVV's own
  • count.**

PART NINE — THE HONEST LIMIT (THE COMMITMENT)

29. The crux: the felt does not, by itself, entail the ground

  • authoritative source owes its reader its limit. The crux is the one raised at the outset: the felt
  • shared with naturalism; the universal-ground interpretation is the Pratyabhijñā's addition, not a
  • nsequence. The felt of one cognition proves the felt exists; it does not, by itself, prove that there
  • one universal consciousness whose felt it is.
  • e IPVV argues the ground more strongly than the secondary literature allows — but it does not force
  • e final step.

30. The IPVV's strongest argument for the ground

  • e IPVV's best argument for the felt→ground step is NOT the assertion of the "one light" (V3C) but the
  • transcendental argument of the order-less support (V2O) plus the causal proof of the one knower**
  • 2P):
"The pratibhā is the flashing — the light that runs through the ordered word-objects, through all
the varied things we name and know. It is seasoned with their order, touched by it. But the flashing
itself is not ordered. Its support — that in which the flashing flashes, the one who knows the order
without being caught in it — is the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower. And that knower is
the great Lord." (V2O)
  • This is a genuine transcendental argument.** Ordered experience is given; but order requires an
  • der-less support — the one who knows the order without being caught in it. You cannot have ordered
  • pearances without the order-less light in which they flash. The one support is not posited arbitrarily;
  • is required by the very structure of ordered experience. And it is confirmed by the causal proof of
  • e one knower (V2P): memory requires the one who remembers — "the valid means is the self-consciousness
  • the one knower." The anvaya-vyatireka (presence-absence): the dealing of the world is fit with the
  • e support, not without it.
  • This DERIVES the need for an order-less, self-conscious support from the structure of ordered,
  • mory-bearing experience.** It is a real argument, not a bare assertion of the "one light."

31. The precise limit

  • t here is the limit, and this source states it plainly:
  • What the IPVV's argument ESTABLISHES: that any ordered, memory-bearing cognition REQUIRES an
  • der-less self-conscious support — a knower who is not caught in the order. This is a strong argument
  • r a transcendental one-support-per-experience (the order-less knower of THIS ordered field).
  • What it does NOT establish: that the order-less knower of one field is numerically identical
  • th the order-less knower of another field. The argument proves each ordered field requires AN
  • der-less support; it does not prove ONE order-less support for all fields.
  • The move from "each field needs an order-less support" to "all fields share one support" requires the
  • rther step** — the argument that the "I" has no counter-correlate (V2C: it is never the object of
  • other, so there is no internal boundary by which one "I"-grasp could be distinct from another). And
  • at step, the IPVV argues but does not force. It is the Śaiva commitment — the point at which the
  • cognition-thesis passes from consequence to wager.
  • e IPVV narrows the gap more than Ratié's reconstruction allows: the order-less support is derived
  • om ordered experience, not merely asserted. But the final universality — the numerical identity of all
  • pports — is the commitment. This is true of the IPK, the IPVV, and Ratié alike; and it is the point at
  • ich the essay's own discipline ("no tradition may inherit another's conclusion merely because they
  • are a structure") requires the argument to stop and mark its boundary. **The felt re-cognition of the
  • lf is established as the removal of a false self-positioning, nothing added; the universalization of
  • at self is the wager the tradition makes and this source holds open.**

  • Ch8 (the other) | V2F, V1L, V2B | 1.1.5, II 4.4/4.9 | other-minds inference refuted; yogipratyakṣa |
  • Ch9 (difference) | V3B, V3E, V3I | II 3.13–14, II 4.17–21 | bhedābheda vimarśa; anti-anirvācya |
  • Conclusion | V3P, V3N/O, V3F | IV 16/18 | the soteriology: dīkṣā, jīvanmukta, guru-paramparā |

33. The deep-dive results

  • Ratié's reconstruction is confirmed in architecture. Every Ratié chapter maps onto an IPVV chunk
  • at argues the same claim with full proof-mechanics. The corrected 1.3.7 (jñāna-smṛti-apoha) is
  • ndicated by the IPVV's own three-vimarśa structure.
  • The IPVV goes further than Ratié in proof, system, and soteriology. Ratié reports; the IPVV
  • roves* (the sārūpya, the two-mirror, the avayavin/paramāṇu, the other-minds inference, the piśāca,
  • e omniscient) and organizes (the vimarśa structure) and completes (the liberation).
  • The IPVV expands the IPK. Every IPK kārikā is unpacked into a running argument with opponents,
  • amples, and doctrinal fixes. The IPK's camatkāra becomes the IPVV's vimarśa = parā-vāk =
  • hurattā = māheśvarya (V2H/I/S).
  • The novelty is ours to quote. The 1.5.11 reflexivity claim, the 1.3.7 triad, the camatkāra/felt
  • gister, the other-as-recognized, freedom-as-essence — all are now citable directly from the IPVV
  • ur translation), the deepest primary source, with the Sanskrit behind them.

34. The conclusion, in the authority's own image

  • e thesis can now be stated with its full support. Recognition is the felt re-cognition of the self:
  • e self, already established, re-cognizes itself as the Lord — the removal of a false self-positioning,
  • d nothing added.
  • The root states it (IPK 1.5.11: the essence of light is the felt reflective awareness; 1.3.7:
  • e three powers; camatkāra as Utpaladeva's own concept).
  • The compass confirms it (Ratié: recognition is experience, not construction; it produces no new
  • owledge; its essence is freedom).
  • The authority argues it — and here the IPVV goes further than Ratié could: it states the thesis
  • three registers (foregrounding, the "I was never not," the lover-union), all one move of
  • ntent-unchanged-positioning-changed; it argues the non-constructed "I" at the root of every
  • gnition; it meets the structural rival not by refutation but by placing the rival's own move inside
  • e intrinsic self-grasp; it co-opts the Buddhist's own tools to its own conclusion; and it expands
  • e IPK into a complete system — action, ontology, soteriology.
  • And it marks its own limit: the felt→ground step is argued (the order-less support) but the final
  • iversalization is the commitment the tradition makes — and this source, holding its own discipline,
  • rks it as a commitment rather than a consequence.
  • e recognition, the IPVV says, is the turning of the un-known nearness into the joy of union. The
  • ver was never absent; the recognition adds nothing; it changes where the self stands, and that change
  • felt. **This is the thesis, in the authority's own image, and it is the thesis of the whole
  • atyabhijñā — argued, not merely asserted, from the deepest source that survives, and shown to expand
  • e IPK and to go further than Ratié's reconstruction.**
